author: kate-waddams
description: Strep throat, a urinary infection, a routine operation: without effective antibiotics, all of it becomes dangerous again. And by overusing them, we are teaching bacteria how to survive them.

hero.hook: By fighting them so hard, we have trained bacteria to survive our medicines.

blocks.text: When bacteria invade our body, the immune system fights back: **white blood cells** attack the infection and we feel better a few days later. But if our defenses are weakened, or overwhelmed, we need backup: antibiotics. A [[bactericidal]] antibiotic destroys the bacterium by attacking its cell wall and its contents; a bacteriostatic one only stops it from multiplying.
Antibiotics are not a modern invention: there is evidence that humans were already using them more than 1,500 years ago, without knowing anything about bacteria.

Depending on the infection, the doctor chooses a **broad-spectrum** antibiotic, active against many species, or a narrow-spectrum one, reserved for a few. Effective, cheap and easy to get, these drugs cover a huge range of infections. That very success is what led the modern world to overuse them. And the bacteria began to fight back.

Antibiotics are among the most transformative advances in modern medicine. They have saved countless lives and we have come to rely on them. But their massive use has created a problem: [[antibiotic resistance]]. Antibiotics that used to kill a bacterium or block its growth no longer work. The bacterium has evolved to outwit the treatment.

blocks.caption: Alexander Fleming, the discoverer of penicillin, in his laboratory.

blocks.text: Evolution is a natural process, and stress from the environment speeds it up. Constantly treating bacteria with molecules designed to kill them amounts to selecting the ones that know how to survive. Their defenses vary: genetic **mutations**, enzymes that dissolve the antibiotic, changes in how they function, and even tiny [[efflux pumps]] that push the drug back out of the cell.

These defenses are written into the genes. When a resistant bacterium divides, it passes them on to its offspring, which pass them on in turn. A single survivor can found a whole line of resistant bacteria. That is how resistance spreads.

A resistant bacterium travels like any other germ. The **Covid** pandemic showed how fast a virus passes from one person, and one country, to the next. Bacteria move the same way: through human contact, in favorable environments, through poor sanitation, or from animals to people.

They also have a shortcut that reproduction does not offer: [[horizontal gene transfer]]. A resistant bacterium can hand its resistance genes directly to a neighbor, without waiting to divide. In very little time, an entire population of resistant bacteria can form this way.

blocks.caption: Clusters of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus seen under an electron microscope.

blocks.text: The best known is [[MRSA]], methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. It stands up to many widely used antibiotics, which earned it the nickname "superbug." Widespread antibiotic use killed off the weaker strains and left the field open to those that, like MRSA, learned to resist. The consequences can be lethal.

sections.title: Genes that travel: the case of MRSA

blocks.text: What does this resistance mean for us? The [[WHO]], the World Health Organization, ranks antimicrobial resistance, meaning resistance to the drugs that fight microbes, antibiotics included, among the **three** biggest public health threats in the world. With fewer and fewer drugs able to fight bacterial infections, all of modern medicine risks becoming less effective.

The numbers show the true scale of the danger. In 2019 alone, **1.27 million** deaths around the world were attributed to antimicrobial resistance. And the curve is still rising: projections put the toll at **10 million** deaths a year by **2050**.

Scientists are not standing idle. They are developing new, more precise treatments that specifically target resistant bacteria. They are also working to restore the effectiveness of existing antibiotics and to cut unnecessary prescriptions: every treatment avoided is one less chance for bacteria to adapt.

sections.title: 1.27 million deaths a year: the WHO's warning

blocks.text: We swallow our antibiotics without a second thought. They are cheap, effective and available everywhere. Without them, a common infection, bacterial **strep throat** or a urinary tract infection, would become much harder to treat. A simple scraped knee could turn into [[sepsis]], a body-wide infection that threatens life.

blocks.caption: A modern operating room: without antibiotics, routine operations would become risky again.

blocks.text: Routine operations, a **cesarean** or a hip replacement, would carry a much higher risk. Antibiotics are often prescribed after surgery to stop an infection from taking hold. Without them, procedures that save or improve lives would become too dangerous to perform.
The future of modern medicine depends on one thing: keeping antibiotics effective, which means no longer overusing them.
